summary: A framework for setting up multimedia sessions where network resource use must be authorized. It explains how session setup, such as with SIP, can be coordinated with quality of service reservations so that the media streams requested stay within the user's service profile and can be accounted for. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a phone call can use special fast lanes, someone has to check you are allowed and keep count of the use. This memo describes how the call setup and the lane reservation can work together.

questions: how do session setup and resource reservation coordinate
how does the framework prevent fraud
what is the role of the authorization token
subtitle: Coordinating call setup with network resource authorization

tldr.problem: When setting up multimedia sessions with quality-of-service requirements, session management (like SIP) and resource reservation (like RSVP) work separately, creating a gap that invites fraud and billing errors. Without linkage, a user could request one media stream but reserve resources for another.
tldr.mechanism: The framework uses an authorization token passed from the policy server through the session management system to the end host, which then includes it in resource reservation requests. The edge router uses the token to verify that requested resources match the authorized media streams.
tldr.outcome: Three models (Coupled, Associated, Non-Associated) describe how different network configurations can link session setup with resource authorization, each with different trust and scalability characteristics.

today: RFC 3521 is an Informational document that describes a framework for coordinating session setup with media authorization. It has not been obsoleted. The framework defined here influenced later standards like RFC 3313 for RSVP extensions to carry authorization tokens.

sections.title: The Problem of Unlinked Authorization
sections.content:
Modern multimedia systems use separate protocols for session management and resource reservation. For example, SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) establishes a call and specifies what media streams are involved, while RSVP (Resource Reservation Protocol) reserves network resources (bandwidth, priority, buffers) to provide quality of service. The problem: these happen independently.

An end host could negotiate a high-quality audio stream with a SIP server, but then request bandwidth for video via RSVP. Without a linkage, the network cannot detect this mismatch. This opens three risks: fraud (a user reserves more resources than authorized), billing errors, and resource exhaustion (resources get locked up for unauthorized uses).

This RFC describes a framework where a policy server authorizes both the media streams and the resources, and uses a token to prove the correlation to the edge router.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine asking permission to make a call and separately asking for a fast lane. If no one checks that both requests are for the same call, someone could get bandwidth they were not allowed, and the bill would be wrong.

sections.title: The Authorization Token Framework
sections.content:
The solution is an authorization token generated by a policy server during the session authorization phase. The token is opaque to most network elements but is designed so that:

1) The policy server can use it to correlate a resource reservation request with the media it authorized earlier. 2) The edge router can use it to determine which policy server made the authorization decision. 3) The token can be cryptographically protected to prevent tampering by untrusted end hosts.

The token flows through the system as follows: the policy server generates it during session setup, includes it in the response to the session management server, the session management server includes it in the response to the end host, and the end host includes it in the resource reservation request sent to the edge router. The edge router uses the token to verify the request with the policy server before admitting resources.
sections.plainLanguage: The policy server creates a voucher that says "this person is allowed to use these resources for this media." The voucher travels with the call setup and resource request, proving that both are for the same authorized session.

sections.title: Network Components and Models
sections.content:
The framework defines a generic network with two domains:

Service Control Domain (SCD): Contains the session management server and a policy server that authorize session requests. It handles call control logic.

Resource Control Domain (RCD): Contains edge routers and a separate policy server that manage packet forwarding and resource admission. It handles data path policy.

The framework describes three models based on how these domains trust each other:

  • Coupled Model: Pre-established trust between all entities (SCD PS, SMS, ER, RCD PS). One policy server handles both domains. Simplest but requires full a priori configuration.
  • Associated Model (One PS): Multiple SMS and ERs, but one PS still serves both domains per transaction. The token must identify which PS authorized it so the ER knows where to query.
  • Associated Model (Two PS) and Non-Associated: Separate policy servers in each domain. The SCD PS and RCD PS must have a trust relationship to coordinate, or there is no assumption of coordination at all (Non-Associated).
sections.plainLanguage: Different network setups trust each other differently. A small private network might use one policy server that everyone trusts. A bigger network might have separate servers for sessions and resources. The framework handles all of these.

sections.title: Token Design and Content
sections.content:
In the Coupled Model, the token's contents are implementation-dependent because only the policy server ever reads it. It can be a simple opaque blob. The policy server secures it to prevent end hosts from tampering.

In the Associated Model with One PS, the token MUST include:

  • Correlation identifier: Lets the PS match the resource request with the earlier media authorization.
  • Identity of the authorizing PS: Lets the ER know which PS to ask about this token.
  • Optionally, authentication data to prevent the ER from being redirected to a bogus PS.

In the Two-PS model, the SCD PS and RCD PS coordinate using the token. The RCD PS must trust the SCD PS to have done the initial authorization.

The token is transparently carried by resource reservation and policy management protocols (RSVP, COPS) as a new opaque object; neither protocol needs to understand its structure.
sections.plainLanguage: The voucher needs to prove two things: that it is tied to one specific authorized session, and (in bigger networks) which policy server issued it. The servers can keep the voucher's details secret; the routers just check that it is valid.

sections.title: Protocol Extensions Required
sections.content:
To implement this framework, three types of protocols need new fields to carry the authorization token:

Resource Reservation Protocol (e.g., RSVP): Needs a new object to carry the token from end host to edge router. The object is opaque to RSVP itself.

Policy Management Protocol (e.g., COPS): Needs a new object to carry the token between policy servers and policy enforcement points. Again, opaque to COPS.

Session Management Protocol (e.g., SIP): Needs a new field to carry the token from the session management server to the end host.

These extensions are protocol-specific. The RFC does not define them (that is left to other documents like RFC 3313 for RSVP extensions). The key principle is that the protocols themselves do not interpret the token; they just ferry it from one endpoint to another.
sections.plainLanguage: Three protocols need to carry the voucher: the call setup protocol carries it to the end host, the resource reservation protocol carries it from the host to the router, and the policy protocol carries it between servers. Each needs a new field, but none need to understand what is inside.
